content.title: Oscars 2026: How to Watch All the Oscar-Nominated Documentaries and Which Will Win
content.text: OSCARS 2026From prison reform in the South to the indoctrination of Russian children living during the invasion of Ukraine, all about the nominated docs at the Oscars 2026.March 11, 2026Andrea Gibson and their wife Megan Falley, the couple at the center of Oscar-nominated documentary Come See Me in the Good Light.The common thread that binds all of the nominated documentaries at Oscars 2026: small acts of bravery with the potential for a big impact. Sara Shahverdi, the first female councilor in her Iranian village, fights for progress against patriarchy in Cutting Through Rocks. Russian school teacher Pavel “Pasha” Talankin documents educational indoctrination during the invasion of Ukraine in Mr. Nobody Against Putin. Incarcerated men expose their prisons’ brutal living conditions via contraband cellphones in The Alabama Solution. Colorado’s former poet laureate Andrea Gibson confronts the final stretch of their four-year cancer battle with wife Megan Falley in Come See Me in the Good Light. And in The Perfect Neighbor, a tight-knit community rallies around a grieving family—and against a local lone wolf with a gun.This year’s nominated documentaries often come with life or death stakes for subjects and filmmakers alike. For anyone looking to catch up on this key category ahead of Sunday’s Academy Awards ceremony (and finish up their Oscar ballot), here is a guide to the five rewarding and societally resonant films, where to watch them, and which might win best documentary at Oscars 2026.The Alabama SolutionDirectors: Andrew Jarecki and Charlotte KaufmanIncarcerated inmates living in one of the deadliest prison systems in the country provided much of the footage in The Alabama Solution. The documentary, from filmmakers behind HBO’s The Jinx, was shot over six years on contraband phones by the men who risked their lives to participate in this film, which unearthed over 1,300 deaths of people in custody inside Alabama correctional facilities between 2019 and 2024.The unflinching documentary casts new light on the more than 21,000 people estimated to be currently in custody in Alabama. During a recent Tonight Show interview, Jarecki invited Alabama governor Kay Ivey and Attorney General Steve Marshall to view the film and respond to its claims. “We reached out to her, and to Steve Marshall, the attorney general, and we said to them, ‘We’d like you to come to Los Angeles—March 14, the day before the Oscars. We’d like you to watch the film with us,’” Jarecki said. “‘And then we’d like you to acknowledge the problem and then come with us and those families to the Oscars’…. We have not heard back yet, but we’re hopeful.”Most PopularLocal news outlet WVTM 13 reached out to Ivey’s office to ask whether she’ll attend a private screening of the film in Los Angeles. “Governor Ivey will be here providing real Alabama solutions to this decades-old challenge that is finally being addressed thanks to her leadership,” a spokesperson for Ivey said in a statement.Come See Me in the Good LightDirector: Ryan WhiteIn the dawning days of a terminal ovarian cancer diagnosis, spoken-word poet Andrea Gibson grapples with the idea of losing their ability to speak alongside their wife, Megan Falley. The ensuing documentary focuses largely on the couple’s unbreakable relationship—as they visit doctors, edit each other’s writing, and prepare for what would become Gibson’s final spoken-word performance in 2024, before their death in July 2025 at the age of 49.Close friend Tig Notaro, who also opened for Gibson’s last performance, produced the film alongside fellow queer celebrities like Brandi Carlile, Abby Wambach, and Glennon Doyle. But for as much as Come See Me in the Good Light—a title taken in part from one of Gibson’s poems—contemplates imminent death, it doesn’t actually show it. “I think Andrea knew this all along and was just kind of waiting for me to understand that this wasn’t going to be a death film, it was going to be a film about living,” White told The Hollywood Reporter of omitting Gibson’s death from the end. “So it was a decision in the edit room: Why does Andrea have to die at the end of this film? It’s not what it’s about.”Cutting Through RocksMost PopularDirectors: Mohammadreza Eyni and Sara KhakiBefore Sara Shahverdi became the first female councilor in her Iranian village, she was a midwife, delivering over 400 babies in her hometown, then fighting for the young girls among them to have better standing in their patriarchal community. As lead councilwoman, Shahverdi advocated for women to co-own property with their husbands and against child marriages—even taking in a 16-year-old girl seeking a divorce from the 35-year-old man she was forced to marry when she was just 12. She does all of this while riding the streets on a motorcycle. “A motorcycle is like a human,” Shahverdi says in the doc. “It faces hardship sometimes. Life is like that.”Shahverdi won’t be able to attend the Oscars 2026 herself due to the US travel ban and the unfolding situation in Iran following the US-Israeli military strikes. “We urge filmmakers and artists to speak out about what is happening in Iran and be on the side of the people of Iran, especially when our film’s lead participant won’t be physically present to speak about it,” the filmmakers recently told Vanity Fair.Khaki and Eyni—the married directors of Cutting Through Rocks—told VF that their “hearts are in two places. We are proud to represent the people of Iran with the first independently made Iranian documentary nominated for an Academy Award, yet we are grieving for our people who are under severe pressure.”(The film is not currently streaming in the US, but is still playing in a limited number of theaters.)(The film is not currently streaming in the US, but is still playing in theaters.)Mr. Nobody Against PutinDirectors: David Borenstein and Pavel Talankin“I love my job, but I don’t want to be a pawn of the regime,” Russian school teacher Pavel “Pasha” Talankin says in Russian, according to English subtitles, in this darkly comic in one moment, then deeply disturbing in another documentary about living under fascist rule. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russian president Vladimir Putin introduced a “federal patriotic education policy,” which overnight saw school curriculum shift in support of the war.Most PopularTalankin is instructed to record the pro-Russia propaganda being taught within his small school in the Chelyabinsk region. But what begins as proof of compliance morphs into an enraged educator’s mission to expose indoctrination of young children through government institutions during war. There is no argument Talankin won’t wage in defense of his students, even sparring with his own mother, the school’s librarian. Talankin left Russia in 2024 before releasing the documentary and relocated to the Czech Republic. He has since traveled in support of Mr. Nobody Against Putin, which already picked up a special jury prize at Sundance 2025 and the BAFTA for best documentary on its way to a potential Oscar upset.Rent on Apple TV or Prime Video or watch with a Kino Film Collection subscriptionThe Perfect NeighborDirector: Geeta GandbhirIn 2023, Black single mother Ajike Owens was killed by her white neighbor Susan Lorincz, who had made regular calls to police complaining about kids playing near her rented Florida property. The following year, Lorincz was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 25 years in prison. She has appealed her conviction.Every pulse-pounding moment leading up to Owens’s killing is documented by police body-cam footage in The Perfect Neighbor. Watching a film told largely through the very same system that failed Owens’s family could make viewers identify too closely with law enforcement, some have argued. “We were really not that concerned with the perspective of the police. They were just the vehicle to showcase this community as they were,” Gandbhir told Vanity Fair in response. “When the police come into communities of color, surveillance can be used to criminalize.” With her documentary, Gandbhir told Vanity Fair, “We wanted it to humanize.”Most PopularWhy It Will Win: The Perfect Neighbor is the best-documentary front-runner not only for its Critics Choice and Independent Spirit Award wins, but also because of the film’s continued social relevance. “When you make a film about a terrible crime, you hope that the film’s relevancy will work itself out of a job. But unfortunately, we see what’s been happening in Minnesota with the murders of Renee Good, Alex Pretti,” Gandbhir told VF. “Masked men who don’t identify themselves, who we sometimes don’t even know if they really are ICE, just kidnapping people off the street and essentially putting them in concentration camps. Body-camera footage should absolutely be required.” According to the National Conference of State Legislatures, only eight states in the US currently require law enforcement to wear body cameras.See What the Oscars 2026 Nominees Wore to Their First Academy Awards1 / 13Steve Granitz/WireImageTimothée Chalamet, 2018In Berluti.Watch the Vanity Fair Oscar Party livestream—hosted by Quenlin Blackwell, Jake Shane, and Brittany Broski—directly after the Academy Awards at youtube.com/vanityfair on Sunday, March 15, 10:30 p.m. ET and 7:30 p.m. PT.See All the Photos From Inside the Vanity Fair Oscar PartySee All the Looks From the Vanity Fair Oscar Party Red CarpetSee All the Looks From the Vanity Fair Oscar Party Red CarpetDid the Academy Get It Right?
